activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Milan went to the store with Mum. He saw a sign on a shelf. It said MILK. Mum read it out loud. The milk was right under the sign. "The word tells us where to look," said Mum. Milan found a blue box with a picture of cereal. He tried to read the letters on it, one by one.

Near the bread, there was a rack of books. Milan found a book about dinosaurs. He opened it at the front. He turned the pages, one at a time, all the way to the back. "I want this book forever," he said. Mum looked at the price. "That is a lot of pennies," she said. "We can borrow one from the library instead."

They walked to the library next door. Milan fetched a dinosaur book from a low shelf. The librarian stamped a little card. "Bring it back on this day," she said, "so other kids can read it too." At home, Milan read the book front to back, twice. On the big day, a leaf began to fall from the tree outside. Milan put the book in his bag. He carried it all the way back to the library, and set it on the desk. "Done," he said.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Ava stood at the door of her classroom. Her tummy felt jumpy. "Will I like school?" she asked her mom. "Yes," said Mom. "And I will wait right here."

Inside, Ava saw a little boy crying. His name was Sam. Ava had a pink bunny in her bag. She pulled it out. She held the bunny up so Sam could see it. Sam stopped crying. He smiled at the bunny.

The teacher put bread and cups on the table for snack time. Ava sat next to Sam. "Bunny makes friends," said Sam. "Yes," said Ava. She learned that a toy can make a sad face turn happy. At the door, Mom waved. Ava waved back with the bunny's soft paw.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Beatrice sat on Grandma's soft rug. She held the black tablet in her lap. Grandma tapped the little button on top. The screen lit up like a morning face.

"Now you try," said Grandma.

Beatrice pressed the button with one finger. The screen went dark. "Oh no," said Beatrice. She pressed it again. The light came back. She laughed. "It sleeps and wakes up!"

Grandma smiled. "What happens if you tap the green ball?"

Beatrice tapped it. The green ball opened into a drawing app. A white page appeared. Beatrice drew a big red circle. Then she drew a yellow sun.

"Can it hold my picture?" asked Beatrice.

"It will wait for you," said Grandma.

Beatrice put the tablet face down on the rug. She picked up her real red ball and rolled it to Grandma.

Later, crumbs fell on the rug. Grandma began to sweep. Beatrice took the tablet to the shelf, just like a big girl.

"Back to sleep," she whispered to the screen.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Lucy wanted tea for her teddy bear. She set him at the little table. "Tea time, friend!" she said.

Dad made the teapot warm. "Careful, it is hot," he said. He poured the tea. Lucy touched the cup with one finger. "Ouch! Hot!" She blew on it. She blew fast. Then she blew slow.

The tea was still too hot. Lucy looked around the playroom. She found a big cup and a small cup. She poured some tea into the small cup. It went wide across her teddy's cup. She touched the small cup. Now it felt cool! The big cup was still hot.

"Teddy, your tea is ready!" said Lucy. She tipped the small cup. The tea went into his cup. Not one drop would spill. Lucy sat up tall. She clapped her hands. "Big cup, slow tea. Small cup, fast tea!"

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Adam went to the playground with his class. He saw the big red truck in the sand. He wanted to play with it.

But Ben had the truck first. Ben filled it with sand. Then he tipped it over. The sand made a big pile.

Adam ran up fast. He grabbed the truck. Ben made a sad face. Adam held the truck tight.

Miss Mia came over. She knelt down beside them. "Ben can have a turn first," she said. "Then you, Adam."

Adam gave the truck back. He sat on the bench. He waited. He watched Ben fill the truck again.

Then Ben walked over to Adam. "Here," said Ben. "Your turn now."

Adam took the truck. He filled it up with sand. He tipped it over. The sand made a big pile, just like Ben's pile.

"Thank you, Ben," said Adam.

Ben smiled a big smile. The two boys played side by side. The playground was noisy with happy kids.

"Truck," said Ben, holding out his hand.

Adam filled it one more time. Then he tipped the sand onto Ben's pile.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Gabriel had one red crayon. His big sister Mia had one blue crayon. They sat at the kitchen table. "I want blue too," said Gabriel. He grabbed Mia's crayon. Mia grabbed it back. The crayon snapped in two. Uh oh.

Now nobody had a whole crayon. Mama came over. She held out her hand. "One at a time," she said softly. "First you, then Mia." Gabriel drew a tight little circle with his red half. Then he gave it to Mia. Mia drew a wiggly snake. She gave it back. "Your turn, Gabriel," she said. Taking turns! The crayon went back and forth, back and forth.

Gabriel laughed. "The crayon tickles my hand when it draws!" The snake grew and grew. It even wore a little hat. At school tomorrow, Gabriel would show Mia's snake to his friends. "Can we draw together?" he asked. Mia smiled and pushed the paper to the middle of the table. "You start," she said.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Norah wants to make pancakes for her family. She gets out eggs, milk and flour. But there is a problem. The butter is cold and hard. Norah tries to stir it. The butter will not stir. "Silly butter," says Norah. "You are too hard!"

Dad says, "Let's give the butter a warm pan." Dad turns on the stove. Norah stands back and watches. Dad drops the butter in the pan. The warm pan makes the butter go soft. Now it is shiny and runny. "It melts!" says Norah. "The warm pan did that!"

Norah stirs the eggs and milk. She stirs the flour too. Dad pours the batter into the pan. The pancakes puff up big and round. Norah gives each pancake a name. "This one is Fluffy. This one is Wobbly. This one is Baby."

The family sits down to eat. Norah passes the shiny pancakes around. "Who wants Baby?" she asks. Baby is gone in one big bite.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Iris sat at the dinner table. She had ten peas on her plate. She wanted to eat them all, but the big ones looked yucky.

"I will count them," said Daddy. "Then they will feel smaller." He pointed at the peas. "One, two, three." Iris giggled. "Four, five, six." She poked a pea with her spoon. "Seven, eight, nine, ten."

Then Daddy ate one pea. "Now you count," he said. Iris pointed too. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine." Her voice sang like a song. Each time she counted, a pea went into her mouth. The big ones did not look yucky anymore. They looked fun.

The clock on the wall gave a little ring. It was near Iris's chair. "Bath time soon," said Mommy. Iris ate her last pea. "One!" she said. Then she held up her spoon like a flag.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Penelope went to the store with Mama. She wanted a banana. "Where do bananas live?" she asked. "Not in the toy part," said Mama.

Penelope looked at the shelves. She saw a teddy bear. The bear did not look like food. She saw a bouncy ball. That was not food either. "Toys go here," she said. "Toys are not for eating."

Then Penelope saw a low shelf with apples. Red apples, round apples. Next to them sat the bananas. She picked one up. "Found it!" she said. Mama smiled. "Good eyes, Penelope."

At the checkout, Penelope saw dog food and cat food. "Is that for me?" she asked. "No, silly," said Mama. "That food is for animals. You are not a puppy." Penelope giggled. "I am not a puppy! I am a girl!" The cashier laughed too. At home, Mama peeled the banana. Penelope took a big bite. "Bananas are food," she said. "The bear stays at the store."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Charles wanted to make a picture for Grandma. He had paper and crayons on the table. He drew a big sun with his orange crayon. Then he wanted to glue on leaves.

Charles found the glue bottle. He squeezed it too hard. A big puddle of glue came out. "Oh no," said Charles. The puddle was wide and shiny. He put a leaf on top of the puddle. The leaf stuck fast to the paper.

Charles touched the glue on his finger. It felt wet and sticky. He waited and looked at his picture. He peeked at his finger again. The glue was not wet anymore. It was dry and stiff. Now his finger felt like paper.

"I need to wash my hands," said Charles. Mom helped him at the sink. Then Charles ran to show Grandma his leaf sun.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Elias went to the mall with Mama. They walked past the toy cars. They walked past the juicy oranges at the fruit stand. Then they came to the hair salon.

"Time for your first haircut," said Mama.

Elias sat in the big chair. It was very tall. The hairdresser, Miss Kim, put a soft cape on him.

"Will it hurt?" asked Elias.

"No," said Miss Kim. "Watch."

She picked up her scissors. Snip, snip. A little piece of hair fell down. It landed on the cape. More snips, and more hair fell, like soft rain.

"Look, Mama!" said Elias. "The scissors make the hair fall down!"

Miss Kim showed him the mirror. His hair was short and neat.

"Nice and cool," said Mama. "Now we can go home and cook dinner."

Elias touched his new hair and smiled at the boy in the mirror.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Mohamed wanted to play house with his bear. But bear looked sad on the floor. His blanket was missing.

"Bear, are you cold?" Mohamed asked. Bear said nothing. "I will fix that."

Mohamed got a small sock. He tucked it around bear like a blanket. Then he held bear close and patted his back. "Shh, shh," he said softly. "Papa is here."

In the kitchen, Mama was making soup. The pot was hot, so Mama held the spoon. Mohamed stayed back and watched. He asked, "Can bear have soup too?" Mama smiled. "Pretend soup is best for bears."

So Mohamed made pretend soup with a cup and water that was not hot. He fed bear one tiny spoon. Bear drank it all up.

Then Mohamed saw something. When he held his cup under the lamp, a shadow grew on the wall. It looked big like a giant cup! He moved the cup. The shadow moved too. "Look, Mama! My cup makes a big shadow!"

Mama laughed. Mohamed finished feeding bear. "Night night, bear," he said. He laid bear down under the sock blanket.

Then he picked up his cup again and made the shadow dance across the wall.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Yesterday Arnaud painted a robot at school. It had big arms and a loud red mouth. But the paint was wet, so it had to stay on the shelf.

Today Arnaud ran to the shelf. "Is it dry now?" he asked. He touched the paper. The paint felt smooth. His robot was done!

Miss Ola smiled. "Now we can fill a frame with it," she said. She held the paper while Arnaud pushed the pins in. He was careful with the sharp pins. Miss Ola pushed them all the way.

The robot hung on the wall. "Tomorrow I want to paint a cat," said Arnaud. "Then the cat will dry too, and later we can hang it next to my robot."

Miss Ola laughed. "A cat and a robot," she said. "That will be a fun wall."

Arnaud looked at the paint pots. He picked up a brush. "Today the cat starts," he said.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Evan sat in the backyard with his friend Mia. They had big paper and cups of paint. Evan had red paint. Mia had blue paint. "Can I use your blue?" Evan asked. "Yes," said Mia. She was polite and shared.

Evan dipped his brush in red. He painted a big apple. Then he dipped in blue. He painted the sky. Then he dipped his brush in blue again. But some yellow paint was still on the brush. Evan looked. The paint turned green on the paper! He gasped. Yellow and blue made green.

He painted green grass all along the bottom. Mia painted green leaves on her tree. Then they painted one picture together. "Red apple, blue sky, green grass," said Evan. Mia laughed and hung it on the fence to dry.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Colton had a library book about boats. He wanted to keep it forever. At bedtime he held it under his arm like a teddy bear.

Mom said, "Time for bed." Colton climbed in. The book sat on his lap. He opened the front cover. On the first page, Mom's finger touched some printed words. "This says borrow," she said. The words were black and smooth under Colton's finger too.

"That means we take it home," Mom said. "But we take it back on Saturday. Then other kids can read it too." Colton looked at the pages. He turned them one by one, front to back. The words went along like little boats floating down a river. He got to the last page. Then the book was done.

Colton's tummy felt funny. He did not want it done. "Can we read it again?" he asked. Mom smiled. "Yes. Read it again and again. Until Saturday comes." Colton turned back to the first page. He could read it many times before then. "Read it again tomorrow," he whispered to the book. Then he turned off his smile, closed his eyes, and held on tight.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Sarah went to the big hall with Mama and Dadu. Tonight was Diwali, the festival of lights. There were little clay lamps everywhere. "One lamp, two lamps, three lamps," Sarah counted. So many lamps!

At the water table, Dadu made a soft paper boat. He set a tiny lamp inside it. Then he set the boat on the water. Would it float? The boat floated! The little light bobbed up and down. Sarah clapped her hands.

"Can my boat have a lamp too?" she asked. A kind aunty helped her fold a soft paper boat. Sarah waited while Dadu lit the small lamp with his match. He was the grown-up, so only he touched it. He placed the lamp in Sarah's boat. Sarah held her boat low, close to the water. Then she let go. The boat floated! But then it spun around and around. "Look, it dances!" said Sarah. The little light danced on the dark water all the way to the other side.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Kinsley wanted to find her red car. She looked in the toy box. She pulled out a blue truck. She pulled out a green frog. No red car.

Kinsley crawled under the little table. She heard a sound. Toot, toot! The red car was stuck way up high on the shelf. Kinsley could not reach it. She jumped. She stretched her arms up. Still no red car.

Mom came in. "Let's get a step stool," said Mom. Mom held the stool steady. Kinsley climbed up one step. She reached and reached. Her fingers touched the red car. It slid down into her hands. "My red car!" said Kinsley.

Kinsley drove the red car on the floor. It bumped into the blue truck. It bumped into the green frog. Then Kinsley found a yellow bus. Now all her cars could play together. The red car went first. "Beep, beep!" said Kinsley.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Norah came home with a small box. Something inside went squeak, squeak. She put the box on the floor. Out came a tiny brown guinea pig. "His name is Bear," Norah said. Her dad helped her pour soft hay into a bowl. Bear nibbled the hay. Crunch, crunch.

Then Bear sat very still. He made a sad little sound. "Maybe he is hungry," Dad said. Norah got a small carrot. She held it out low. Bear sniffed it. Then he took a bite. His whiskers wiggled. Norah laughed.

After the carrot, Bear made a happy pop sound. He jumped up, all four feet in the air. "He popped!" Norah said. Dad smiled. "Carrots make him jump for joy." Bear curled up in the hay, warm and small. Norah patted him soft, soft, soft. "Good night, Bear," she whispered.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Weston ran to the playground with Dad. He felt so excited. The slide was big and tall. Weston wanted to slide down it fast.

He climbed up the steps. A big dog barked loud. Weston felt scared. He held the rail tight. Dad came close and held his hand. "The dog is on a leash," said Dad. "You are safe." Weston looked at the dog. The dog wagged its tail and sat down.

Weston slid down the tall slide. Whee! He laughed and felt happy. Then a girl took the swing he wanted. Weston felt angry. His face got hot. Dad said, "Take a breath. Ask for a turn." Weston took a big breath. "Can I have a turn?" he asked. The girl said, "Yes, when I count to ten."

Then came the surprise. The girl jumped off the swing. She pulled a red balloon from her pocket. "It is for you," she said. Weston had not seen it there. He hugged the balloon and smiled big. "I think I like this park," said Weston. Dad lifted him up high. "Swing time," said Dad. Weston held the balloon tight and kicked his feet.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Juliette sat at the art table. She wanted to make a picture for her mama. But her paper was empty. She waited and looked at the tray.

The teacher held a big brown potato. "This is a root," she said. "It grows under the ground." The teacher cut it with a knife. Juliette watched from her seat. Now the potato had a flat top. The teacher cut one into a circle. She cut one into a square. She cut one into a triangle. She cut one into a rectangle.

Juliette dipped the circle in red paint. She pressed it on the paper. She lifted it up. A red circle stayed there! She pressed hard again. Another circle appeared.

She stamped the square in blue. Four flat sides. She stamped the triangle in yellow. Three pointy corners. She stamped the rectangle in green. Long and flat.

Then she licked a bit of paint on her finger. "Yuck," said Juliette. "Paint does not taste good."

She made a house with the square. She made a roof with the triangle. She made a sun with the circle. She made a door with the rectangle.

The picture was full of shapes. Juliette held it up to the window. The sun shone through the paper. "Look," she said. "A house for you, Mama."

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Zoey sat in the big waiting chair. Today she would get her first haircut. Her hair was long. It kept falling in her eyes. She pushed it away. It fell back again.

"Zoey," called a lady named Miss Kim. Zoey walked over and climbed into the tall salon chair. Miss Kim gave her a cape to wear. It was blue like the sky.

Miss Kim sprayed water on Zoey's hair. The wet hair stuck down flat. It did not fall in Zoey's eyes anymore. Then Miss Kim used her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Zoey sat very still. She watched little pieces of hair drop onto the cape.

Soon the haircut was done. Zoey looked in the mirror. She could see her whole face. No hair was in her eyes. "I did it," said Zoey. Miss Kim clapped. Mommy said, "You were so brave." After that, they went home to get dinner. Zoey made a sour face at the green beans, but she smiled at her new short hair in the window.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Oliver went to the big hall with Mama and Grandpa. Today was the lantern festival. Lanterns hung from the ceiling like pretty orange moons. Oliver wanted to find the red one with a dragon on it. Grandpa had helped him buy it at the little shop last week.

But the red dragon lantern was not lit. All the other lanterns glowed. His stayed dark. Oliver held Grandpa's hand and walked closer. The lantern had a small candle inside. Grandpa bent down. He used a long match to light it. A grown-up helper watched and nodded.

Then the candle made a warm glow. The dragon's wings turned bright gold. Oliver could feel little heat on his fingers when he leaned close. Grandpa pulled him back a step, just to be safe.

A girl next to them looked sad. Her paper fan had a tear in it. Oliver showed her his glowing dragon. She smiled big. She whispered, "That one is my secret favorite." Oliver grinned and said, "Mine too." The lanterns swayed above them, all shining together.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Violet ran to the window at daycare. Yesterday the class had planted seeds in little pots. Teacher Sam had poured the dirt for them. Violet had pushed one seed down with her finger.

Now the pots sat on the sunny sill. The dirt looked plain and brown. "Where is my plant?" Violet asked.

"It is not now," said Teacher Sam. "It grows later. First we water it today."

Violet held her small cup. She poured the cold water slowly onto her pot. The dirt turned dark. A tiny drip ran down the side of the pot. Her friend Milo watered his pot too.

Then it was playtime. Then it was snack time. Then Daddy came. Violet looked back at the sill. The dirt was still plain and brown.

"Come back tomorrow," said Teacher Sam. "The seed wakes up after it drinks."

The next day Violet ran to the window first thing. There, in her pot, was a small green loop. It had pushed up through the dirt.

"Look!" said Violet. "It came!"

"Because you watered it yesterday," said Teacher Sam.

Violet touched the tiny leaf with one careful finger.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Aubrey wanted to make her own breakfast. Daddy put warm toast on her plate. The butter sat in a little dish beside it.

"Can I do it?" Aubrey asked. Daddy gave her a dull, safe spreader. She pushed the butter. It made a big lump in one spot. She tried again. The lump slid around and around. Then she held the spreader flat and moved it slow. The lump turned into a smooth, shiny coat. "Look! It went all smooth!" she said.

Next came the milk. Aubrey held the cup with both hands. She poured too fast, and milk ran over the rim. She stopped. How slow is slow? She tipped the jug a tiny bit. The milk went in drop by drop. The cup stayed dry. She poured the second cup for Daddy the same way. Not one drop spilled.

Aubrey took a big bite of her toast. "I can do it myself," she said. Daddy held up his cup. "To my big helper!"

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Felix stood on his stool at the big kitchen table. The toast was warm and golden. Miss Amy put a small pat of butter on top. "Now you," she said.

Felix picked up the soft butter knife. He spread one way. Then he spread the other way. The butter melted a little and went smooth. One, two, three, slow. The toast shined all over. "I did it!" said Felix.

Next came the milk. Felix poured fast. Milk splashed onto the table. Miss Amy wiped it with a cloth. "Try again," she said. Felix tipped the cup just a tiny bit. One, two, three, slow. The milk went in and did not spill.

After snack time, they would buy apples for tomorrow. Miss Amy said the market was by the beach. Felix's sock felt itchy, so she helped him pull it straight. Then he lifted his cup with two hands and took a big, careful sip.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Evan wanted to paint a picture at daycare. He looked for his favorite color. It was red. The red paint pot was empty.

"Can I help?" asked Miss Kim. She squeezed the tube. A little red paint came out. It was not enough. Evan had an idea. He put yellow paint on his brush. Then he added red on top. The colors mixed on the paper.

"Look!" said Evan. The paint turned orange. Miss Kim smiled. "That is neat," she said. Evan hurried to try more. Blue and yellow made green. His friend Sam came to look.

"Wow," said Sam. "Can I try too?" Evan gave Sam the yellow brush. Sam added blue. Green filled the page.

Miss Kim hung both pictures by the window. The orange sun and the green grass shone in the light.

"I made sun colors," said Evan.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Grandma drove Ruby to her house for lunch. Ruby was hungry. She saw the soup and reached for her spoon.

"Not yet," said Grandma. "First we say our words." Grandma folded her hands. "Thank you for our food," she said. Grandpa said it too. Then they picked up their spoons.

Ruby tried. "Thank you for our soup," she said. Grandma clapped. Grandpa clapped. Then everyone ate.

After lunch, Ruby had a nap on the fuzzy blanket. When she woke up, Grandpa put out bread and butter.

"Wait," said Ruby. She folded her hands. "Thank you for our bread." Grandpa laughed and picked up his knife. Grandma picked up hers.

"More bread, please," said Ruby, and she took a big piece.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Mason stood by the bus door. He held his mama's hand tight. The bus was big and yellow.

Mason wanted to sit by the window. But he did not know where to go. A big kid sat down fast. The seat by the window was full.

Mason walked down the aisle. He found a seat with room. He sat by the window after all. "Hi," said a girl next to him. Her name was Nia.

Mason looked out the window. He saw his mama wave. Mason waved back. Then he pressed his hand on the glass. The glass was cold and smooth. Nia saw him and pressed her hand too. Two hands, one on each side of a little mark.

The bus door closed with a whoosh. The driver turned a handle to lock it. The bus began to roll. Mama got smaller and smaller. Mason made a happy face at her. Then he looked at Nia. "Want to see my truck?" he asked. Nia nodded. Mason opened his backpack and pulled it out.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Amelia stood at the paint table in the art room. She wanted to paint a purple grape. But there was no purple paint. Not one drop.

She looked at the pots. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. There was blue paint. "Red, yellow, blue," she said, pointing at each pot. Those were the three big colours.

Her teacher, Miss Jo, smiled. "Try putting two colours together," said Miss Jo. "See what your brush can do."

Amelia dipped her brush in the blue. Then she dipped it in the red. She swirled them on her paper. The red and blue began to mix. Round and round went her brush. The paint turned purple!

"My grape!" said Amelia. She painted one big purple grape. Then she painted five more.

Tom peeked over from the next table. "I want purple too," he said.

"You need red and blue," said Amelia. She held up her brush like a magic wand. "Ta-da!"

Tom mixed his colours. His paint turned purple too. "We match!" he said.

Amelia looked at the yellow pot. She wondered about yellow and blue. She tried it. Green! Like grass! Like a frog!

"Next time I will paint a frog," said Amelia. She put her purple painting in her favorite spot on the drying rack.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Ryan sat at the little desk in the library. He wanted to write his name. But the pencil kept slipping. His R looked like a wiggly worm.

Miss Jo, the library lady, put a small pencil in his hand. "Try a pinch," she said softly. "Pinch it like this." She showed him. Ryan pinched the pencil with two fingers.

The pencil stopped wiggling. Ryan made a line. The line was straight! He made a big R. It looked like a real R.

Ryan made a sour face at the crooked y. Then he pinched again. The y came out neat too.

"Can I do the a?" Ryan asked. He thought about his pinch. He wrote a, then n. The pencil went where he told it to go.

Miss Jo put his paper on the wall. Ryan pointed at it. "That one is mine!"

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Grayson woke up and looked out the window. The world was white. "Snow!" he said. No school today. It was a snow day at home.

Grayson wanted to build a snow hill. He scooped snow into his bowl. He carried it to his room. He patted it into a big pile on his tray. Then he flew his toy plane over the top. "Up, up!" he said. The plane went over the bumpy hill. But then Grayson saw something. The hill was getting small. Little drops sat on the tray. The room was warm, and the snow was turning to water.

Grayson ran to Mom. "My hill is going away!" he said. Mom smiled. "Fill your bowl again," she said. "We can build it outside." Grayson put on his boots and coat. Mom helped with his zipper. Outside, they patted the snow into one big hill. Grayson flew his plane up and down. He clapped his mittens together. "The hill stays big out here!" he said. Mom laughed and patted more snow for him.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Felix stood by the wooden fence at school. He did not know anyone yet. He held his red ball very tight.

A boy ran past. The boy had a big truck. Felix wanted to play. But he did not know how to start.

Then his ball slipped out of his hands. It rolled down the hill. It rolled fast, fast, fast. Felix ran after it. The ball rolled right to the boy with the truck. It stopped next to the truck. The sand caught it. The boy picked it up. He rolled it back. Felix rolled it to him again. The sand caught it again.

"You can play with us," said the boy. Felix smiled big. He gave the boy a picture he had drawn. It was a picture of a red ball.

At home, Felix would remember this day. But now it was time to play. The ball rolled again.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Isabella went to Miss Dot's music room. Miss Dot had a big drum and a shiny silver bell. "Today we will clap," said Miss Dot. Isabella wanted to clap very fast. She clapped clap-clap-clap-clap like rain!

But the drum went slow. Boom... boom... boom. Isabella's claps ran ahead. Then her claps got all mixed up. "My hands are silly," said Isabella. Miss Dot laughed. "Make your hands wait," she said. "Listen first."

So Isabella watched the drum. Boom. Her hands went boom too. Clap. Boom. Clap. Boom. It was the same! When the drum went slow, she clapped slow. When Miss Dot tapped faster, Isabella clapped faster too. "One, two, one, two," said Miss Dot, and Isabella's hands followed all by themselves.

Then they sang "Twinkle, Twinkle." Miss Dot pointed to a toy cat on the piano. "Sing it to him," she said. Isabella sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." The cat's tail stuck straight up. "He likes it," said Miss Dot. Isabella sang louder. "How I wonder what you are!" Miss Dot hit the shiny bell one time. Ding! The cat jumped, and Isabella fell down laughing. "Again," she said. "Again, again, again!"

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Zachary stood in the school computer lab. He wanted to draw a big blue pond. But the tablet was dark. "I can't see anything," he said.

Miss Ruiz sat next to him. "Just press the round button," she said. "Be careful and press it soft." Zachary pressed the button. The screen lit up. He smiled. The light made the dark go away. Then he tapped the little paint pot picture. The drawing app opened. He drew a blue pond with green frogs. Then he tapped a duck and gave it a yellow beak.

"Now I want a new one," he said. "First we put it away," said Miss Ruiz. She helped him tap the home square. The screen went calm. "Can we sell my duck picture at the art show?" he asked. Miss Ruiz laughed. "Let's print it first," she said, and Zachary clapped his hands.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma was coming to stay for a whole week. Elizabeth had a job to do. She had to make the guest bed ready.

Elizabeth put a soft blanket on the bed. She put a pillow at the top. "One blanket, one pillow, one cozy bed," she said. But the bed still did not look right. It looked flat and sad.

Then Elizabeth had an idea. She grabbed the blanket and fluffed it up. She puffed the pillow with both hands. The bed got soft and puffy, like a big nest. "Now it looks like a nest," said Elizabeth. "A tight, warm nest."

Grandma came in with her little brown bag. She touched the puffy blanket. She sat down on the soft bed. "Oh, this is lovely," said Grandma. "The puffy blanket makes the bed warm. I love it."

"One blanket, one pillow, one happy Grandma," said Elizabeth. She gave Grandma a hug.

Grandma patted the bed. "Come sit with me." Elizabeth climbed up next to her. They sat in the nest together, snug and still.

knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Jasmine went to the park with her dad. The sun was out. It was sunny. She wore her shiny red hat. The wind began to blow. It was windy. The wind took her hat right off her head!

"Can I get my hat?" she asked. Dad said, "Yes, let's chase it together."

The hat rolled and rolled. Then dark clouds came. Rain fell. It was rainy. The rain made the hat wet and heavy. The hat stopped rolling. Jasmine picked it up.

"Why did it stop?" she asked. "The rain made it wet," said Dad.

Then something soft and white fell from the sky. It was snow. Jasmine laughed. Snow landed on her neck. Dad put her warm coat on her. The coat was cozy.

Jasmine put the wet hat in the bag. She held Dad's hand. "Snowy parks are cold," she said, "but warm coats are just right." Dad smiled and said, "Home for hot cocoa."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Mohamed had a library book. It was about a turtle. The turtle had a green shell. Mohamed loved the turtle book so much.

"Can I keep it forever?" he asked Daddy.

"No," said Daddy. "We borrowed it. We take it back soon. Then other kids can read it too."

Mohamed held the book tight. He opened the front cover. He turned the pages one by one. He saw little black marks on the page. "What are those?" he asked.

"Those are words," said Daddy. "Words tell the story."

Daddy pointed to a word. "That says turtle." Mohamed looked. The marks did look a bit like a little turtle walking! He turned more pages. The turtle in the story found a leaf. The turtle ate the leaf. Then the turtle began to grow, bigger and bigger.

Mohamed turned the page again. Then the pages ran out. The back cover was hard and smooth. "The end," said Daddy. Mohamed patted the back cover.

The next morning, Mohamed spun in a circle. He spun and spun. Then he felt dizzy and fell down on the rug, laughing. Daddy laughed too. "Time to go," said Daddy. "The book goes back today."

At the library, Mohamed gave the book to the lady at the desk. She smiled and put it on a shelf. Another little girl picked it up right away. She sat down and opened the front cover.

Mohamed peeked at her. "That page says turtle," he whispered to Daddy.

"Do you want another book to take home?" Daddy asked.

Mohamed nodded. "One about a turtle that grows," he said. He ran to the shelf.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Samuel ran out to the backyard in the morning. The sun was out. "It is sunny today," he said. He put on his sun hat. Then he began to build a tower of blocks on the grass. But the wind blew. The wind blew and blew. The hat flew off his head! "Wind, why did you take my hat?" The wind did not answer. It just kept blowing. So Samuel went inside and put on his warm coat. Now the wind could not touch him.

Soon the sky turned gray. Rain fell on the blocks. Plip, plip, plip. "Rain, rain, where will you go?" The rain went down into the grass. Samuel watched from the porch. It was quiet in the rain. He clapped his hands. Then small white flakes came down too. "Mama, what is that?" Mama smiled. "That is snow." The snow made the blocks all white.

Samuel put on his mittens and his boots. He stepped into the soft snow. His boots made little marks. He picked up the snowy blocks one by one. "I will build a snow tower," he said. The snow stuck to the blocks and made them stick together. His tower stood tall and white. Samuel patted the top. "Snowy tower, hello." Mama stood by the door and waved. Samuel waved back and said, "Hello, Mama. Come see my snow tower."

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story: Naomi wanted to make a house for Teddy. She looked at her blocks on the soft rug. First she tried the circle block. It rolled away. Thump, thump, across the floor. "Come back," said Naomi. The square block did not roll. It sat still. She stacked four squares. The walls grew tall. Naomi clapped her hands. Then she held up a triangle. It looked like a little roof. She set it on top. The house had a pointy hat now. Teddy is thirsty, Naomi thought. She found her rectangle block. It lay flat like a little table. She put a toy fork and a tiny cup on it. "Drink your water, Teddy," she said. The circle block rolled back and bumped her toe. Naomi laughed and picked it up. "You can be the moon," she told it. She held the circle up high above the house. It hung there in her hand, round and shiny, like a night light. Naomi yawned and sat down. "Time for bed, Teddy," she whispered.

story:
Wyatt waits at the bus stop with Grandma. He wants to see the bus come. But no bus comes yet. The sun is out. It is sunny. Wyatt takes off his hat. "Too hot," he says.

Then the wind blows. It is windy now. The wind takes Wyatt's hat and rolls it down the street. "Come back, hat!" says Wyatt. Grandma laughs. They run and get the hat. Grandma puts it back on his head. She zips his coat up to his chin. "The wind is sharp today," she says.

Then the sky turns gray. Rain drops fall. It is rainy now. Grandma opens a big umbrella. Pop! The rain goes plip, plip on top. Wyatt holds Grandma's hand under the umbrella. "Bus!" he shouts. The big yellow bus rolls up. "Bus, bus, bus!"
